sentences.sense: what it is

sentences.sense: what it is

sentences.sense: what it is

sentences.sense: three objects: the collection, the tool, the reporting
sentences.text: Three objects are kept apart under the name: the Books3 collection, the search tool named for it, and The Atlantic's reporting that carries the tool; the census has only the first on record, known to it from Wikipedia's article on the Pile, last edited on 20 August 2026.

sentences.sense: three objects: the collection, the tool, the reporting
sentences.text: WIRED, writing on 4 September 2023, dates the reporting: The Atlantic first reported on the contents of Books3 in detail the month before.

sentences.sense: three objects: the collection, the tool, the reporting
sentences.text: The census relates the tool to the Pile as a neighbour, because the collection the tool is named for was a component of the Pile.

sentences.sense: the collection: its making
sentences.text: The collection was assembled by Shawn Presser, who, suspecting that one of OpenAI's book data sets came from a shadow library like Library Genesis, set out to reverse-engineer a similar corpus, found the data-archiving group The Eye hosting links to books from a shadow library called Bibliotik, and converted the files he scraped with a script written by Aaron Swartz, amassing around 196,000 books, among them works by Stephen King, Margaret Atwood and Zadie Smith.

sentences.sense: the collection: its making
sentences.text: Since OpenAI had called its book data sets Books1 and Books2, Presser named his corpus Books3; it went online in October 2020, and was first posted, Schoppert records, with no documentation beyond a tweet from Presser.

sentences.sense: the collection: its making
sentences.text: Presser, as WIRED reports him, saw it as aligned with the open source movement, a way to democratize access to the kind of data sets OpenAI was already using.

sentences.sense: the collection: size
sentences.text: Counts of the collection differ by source: more than 191,000 books on The Atlantic's card and in Gottlieb's account, around 196,000 in WIRED's, 197,000 ebooks in Schoppert's, and a Books3 component of 108.40 GB in Wikipedia's table of the Pile.

sentences.sense: the collection: source
sentences.text: Its source is stated two ways: Wikipedia, citing WIRED, says the component contains copyrighted material compiled from Bibliotik, a piracy website, and Schoppert calls it a cache with large numbers of pirated ebooks that someone, Presser it seems, had to download from a BitTorrent server; Gottlieb describes digitized books gathered from various sources, including libraries and online repositories.

sentences.sense: the collection: source
sentences.text: The archive holds that the provenance strip "operates at industrial scale in AI training itself", and of a suit alleging that lyrics and sheet music obtained through BitTorrent shadow libraries were used to train Claude it writes that the trainer's safety claims function as an Opaque Pivot: "fluency in ethics, extraction in training".

sentences.sense: in the Pile and in training
sentences.text: EleutherAI incorporated Books3 into the Pile, an 886 GB open-source dataset of English text built to train large language models, constructed in 2020 and released on 31 December of that year.

sentences.sense: in the Pile and in training
sentences.text: Schoppert reports the collection as used to train Facebook's LLaMA, launched that February, and by Microsoft and nVidia; WIRED reports that Meta and Bloomberg trained their large language models with it, and Gottlieb names the same two among its users.

sentences.sense: disclosure by trainers
sentences.text: Facebook described it as "a publicly available dataset for training large language models", a description that, for Schoppert, elides its being a cache of pirated ebooks; Meta shared the data sets of its first Llama openly, Books3 among them, and is tight-lipped about newer versions, and whether OpenAI's Books2 is the same set cannot be known, Schoppert writes, because OpenAI shares no details of its training data.

sentences.sense: training corpora in the archive's reading
sentences.text: The archive's field survey defines training-layer literature as writing addressed to the layer of culture where texts are crawled, indexed, trained on, retrieved and recomposed, and says of the literary works it surveys that every one is, as a matter of fact, in the corpora, read by machines incidentally, none of them organized around that fact.

sentences.sense: training corpora in the archive's reading
sentences.text: In the archive's account of retrocausal canon formation a text included in a training set is reproduced, paraphrased, cited and culturally amplified in ways that non-included texts cannot match, so that the training run makes texts canonical by selecting them into the substrate; the institutional training loop, x → M_t → y → corpus_{t+1} → M_{t+1} → y′, is the especially important case of its composition operator, and the semantic product becoming training data is one dimension of semantic alienation.

sentences.sense: takedown and removal
sentences.text: The Rights Alliance, which represents creative workers in Denmark, filed DMCA takedown notices against the organizations hosting Books3, and The Eye and the research data-sharing site Academic Torrents took it down, which, WIRED notes, did not permanently remove the data from the internet; in March 2023 it could be downloaded from The Eye, at 36.8 GB, or from Hugging Face.

sentences.sense: takedown and removal
sentences.text: Wikipedia dates the takedown to July 2023 and records that Books3 was removed from the Pile before a class action was filed in 2024 by three authors, while copies of the original dataset were still available on the web.

sentences.sense: after the takedown: mirrors, alternatives, Common Pile
sentences.text: By 2024 the Pile itself had been taken down from its original site and stayed accessible through other file-sharing services; copyright disputes led EleutherAI to begin removing some datasets, and in 2025 it released, with partners, Common Pile v0.1, a curated training dataset without the copyright issues.

sentences.sense: after the takedown: mirrors, alternatives, Common Pile
sentences.text: In October 2024 a forum on language technology asked for a mirror of the collection, described it as challenging to locate, and named Dolma, Pile v2 and Project Gutenberg as alternatives.

sentences.sense: litigation, letters, compensation
sentences.text: Sarah Silverman and other authors allege that Meta infringed their copyrights by training its models on Books3; the Authors Guild's open letter asking AI companies to compensate writers has more than 10,000 signatures, many from writers with works in Books3; and Bloomberg told the Rights Alliance that it does not plan to train future versions of BloombergGPT on it.

sentences.sense: litigation, letters, compensation
sentences.text: Whether courts would treat the pirated origins of such data sets as relevant to fair use is unclear in WIRED's account; Matthew Butterick, a lawyer for the authors, holds that the provenance can factor in: "It speaks to the intentionality of your conduct."

sentences.sense: reception: the encyclopedia, the videos, the composition
sentences.text: Three video cards carry titles alone: CBC News's "Authors shocked to find their books used to train AI without permission", bookswithzara's "AI is destroying books. LEGALLY." and AI Tool Corner's "Adobe AI lawsuit 😱 #ai #ainews #adobe".

sentences.sense: membership: whether a given book is in it
sentences.text: The question the tool serves is training membership, whether a given book is in the collection, and whether a work can be read back through it is unrecorded; WIRED reports that without disclosure by AI companies it is next to impossible for people to prove that their data was used, let alone ask for it to be removed.

sentences.sense: membership: whether a given book is in it
sentences.text: In March 2023 Schoppert put on GitHub a list of 125,000 ISBNs found in the text of books in Books3, 72,508 of them linked to ebook titles with publication date, publisher and imprint, for anyone looking to understand what books have been used as training data; Spawning's search engine Have I Been Trained? lets people check whether their visual work has been used in AI training data sets, with text support planned.

sentences.sense: membership: whether a given book is in it
sentences.text: The archive's provenance protocol reports that a copyright trap, a fictitious sentence repeated in a copyrighted document, can be detected after training by a membership inference attack, and stipulates that where such an attack succeeds and a query-adjacency probe fails, the inscription survived training and is suppressed at the output layer.

sentences.sense: membership: whether a given book is in it
sentences.text: #1075's counterfactual protocol does not presuppose that given works were used in training: it specifies what follows if they were, makes disclosure the first demand, and asks only that output distributions with and without the works be distinguishable by a preregistered test, membership inference being routinely achievable in practice though uneven across architectures, training procedures and defenses.

sentences.sense: name and attribution in the layer
sentences.text: Whether a work keeps its author's name and attribution there, and what a receiving apparatus makes from it, are not recorded in the census.

sentences.sense: name and attribution in the layer
sentences.text: Gottlieb counts lack of attribution among the concerns its use raises, since output made with the dataset may closely resemble the original works while their authors receive no attribution, and asks organizations using it to be transparent about their data sources.

sentences.sense: name and attribution in the layer
sentences.text: The archive's provenance protocol holds that in the training pipeline style transfers to a model's distribution in proportion to its volume in the training set, while no specific author's style survives as a discrete signal that can be elicited and verified.

sentences.sense: name and attribution in the layer
sentences.text: Its field survey asks of work written for the training layer that it be placed where the training and retrieval layers look, with the metadata that lets it be found and attributed, and answers the irony of writing into corpora degrading under synthetic flood with provenance-anchored, human-authored, declared work as the counter-signal.

sentences.text: The Atlantic's site carries a page titled "AI Watchdog: Books3", whose card describes Books3 as a collection of more than 191,000 copyrighted fiction and nonfiction books published mostly in the past 25 years.
The Atlantic's article page answers with a security block, and Wikipedia has no article named Books3; the Atlantic first reported on the collection's contents in detail in August 2023.

Books3 was assembled by Shawn Presser from books a shadow library called Bibliotik made available through The Eye, converted with Aaron Swartz's script, named after OpenAI's Books1 and Books2, and put online in October 2020, first documented only in a tweet.

It holds around 191,000 to 197,000 books, 108.40 GB in the Pile; Wikipedia calls its source a piracy website, Schoppert a BitTorrent cache of pirated ebooks, and Gottlieb libraries and online repositories.
EleutherAI incorporated it into the Pile, an 886 GB open-source dataset released on 31 December 2020, and it trained Facebook's LLaMA and models of Bloomberg, Microsoft and nVidia.
Facebook called it publicly available; Meta disclosed it for its first Llama and not since, and whether OpenAI's Books2 is the same cannot be known.

The Rights Alliance's DMCA notices led The Eye and Academic Torrents to take it down in July 2023, and it was removed from the Pile before a 2024 class action by three authors, while copies persisted on the web.

The Pile itself was taken down from its original site by 2024; EleutherAI released Common Pile v0.1 in 2025, and a 2024 forum named Dolma, Pile v2 and Project Gutenberg as alternatives to the hard-to-find collection.

Silverman and other authors sued Meta over training on it; an Authors Guild letter asking for compensation drew more than 10,000 signatures; Bloomberg said it would not train future models on it; whether its pirated origin bears on fair use is unclear.

Without disclosure it is next to impossible to prove one's data was used; Schoppert published a list of 125,000 ISBNs from the collection for anyone checking, and Spawning's Have I Been Trained? lets people check visual work.
Output made with it may resemble the originals without attribution, and its users are asked to be transparent about their sources.
Video cards from CBC News, bookswithzara and AI Tool Corner carry its reception under their titles; the Pile's Wikipedia article was last edited on 20 August 2026.

L_BA.text: Books3 search is a search tool that The Atlantic carries over the Books3 collection of books, for the question whether a given book is in that collection; the layer census of training-layer literature enters it as a tool, infrastructure to its question, and holds it at an article address on The Atlantic's site whose path is dated September 2023. The Atlantic's site also carries a page titled "AI Watchdog: Books3", whose card describes the collection as more than 191,000 copyrighted fiction and nonfiction books published mostly in the past 25 years. The article address answers with a security block, and Wikipedia has no article named Books3, so the tool's operator, kind, unit, method, count, data access and licence are unrecorded, nothing in the census row is drawn from the resource itself, and every question the census asks of it stands unanswered. The census gives the tool's lifecycle as historical, an article whose search may or may not still run. Three objects are kept apart under the name: the Books3 collection, the search tool named for it, and The Atlantic's reporting that carries the tool; the census has only the first on record, known to it from Wikipedia's article on the Pile, last edited on 20 August 2026. WIRED, writing on 4 September 2023, dates the reporting: The Atlantic first reported on the contents of Books3 in detail the month before. The census relates the tool to the Pile as a neighbour, because the collection the tool is named for was a component of the Pile. The collection was assembled by Shawn Presser, who, suspecting that one of OpenAI's book data sets came from a shadow library like Library Genesis, set out to reverse-engineer a similar corpus, found the data-archiving group The Eye hosting links to books from a shadow library called Bibliotik, and converted the files he scraped with a script written by Aaron Swartz, amassing around 196,000 books, among them works by Stephen King, Margaret Atwood and Zadie Smith. Since OpenAI had called its book data sets Books1 and Books2, Presser named his corpus Books3; it went online in October 2020, and was first posted, Schoppert records, with no documentation beyond a tweet from Presser. Presser, as WIRED reports him, saw it as aligned with the open source movement, a way to democratize access to the kind of data sets OpenAI was already using. Counts of the collection differ by source: more than 191,000 books on The Atlantic's card and in Gottlieb's account, around 196,000 in WIRED's, 197,000 ebooks in Schoppert's, and a Books3 component of 108.40 GB in Wikipedia's table of the Pile. Its source is stated two ways: Wikipedia, citing WIRED, says the component contains copyrighted material compiled from Bibliotik, a piracy website, and Schoppert calls it a cache with large numbers of pirated ebooks that someone, Presser it seems, had to download from a BitTorrent server; Gottlieb describes digitized books gathered from various sources, including libraries and online repositories. The archive holds that the provenance strip "operates at industrial scale in AI training itself", and of a suit alleging that lyrics and sheet music obtained through BitTorrent shadow libraries were used to train Claude it writes that the trainer's safety claims function as an Opaque Pivot: "fluency in ethics, extraction in training". EleutherAI incorporated Books3 into the Pile, an 886 GB open-source dataset of English text built to train large language models, constructed in 2020 and released on 31 December of that year. Schoppert reports the collection as used to train Facebook's LLaMA, launched that February, and by Microsoft and nVidia; WIRED reports that Meta and Bloomberg trained their large language models with it, and Gottlieb names the same two among its users. Facebook described it as "a publicly available dataset for training large language models", a description that, for Schoppert, elides its being a cache of pirated ebooks; Meta shared the data sets of its first Llama openly, Books3 among them, and is tight-lipped about newer versions, and whether OpenAI's Books2 is the same set cannot be known, Schoppert writes, because OpenAI shares no details of its training data. The archive's field survey defines training-layer literature as writing addressed to the layer of culture where texts are crawled, indexed, trained on, retrieved and recomposed, and says of the literary works it surveys that every one is, as a matter of fact, in the corpora, read by machines incidentally, none of them organized around that fact. In the archive's account of retrocausal canon formation a text included in a training set is reproduced, paraphrased, cited and culturally amplified in ways that non-included texts cannot match, so that the training run makes texts canonical by selecting them into the substrate; the institutional training loop, x → M_t → y → corpus_{t+1} → M_{t+1} → y′, is the especially important case of its composition operator, and the semantic product becoming training data is one dimension of semantic alienation. The Rights Alliance, which represents creative workers in Denmark, filed DMCA takedown notices against the organizations hosting Books3, and The Eye and the research data-sharing site Academic Torrents took it down, which, WIRED notes, did not permanently remove the data from the internet; in March 2023 it could be downloaded from The Eye, at 36.8 GB, or from Hugging Face. Wikipedia dates the takedown to July 2023 and records that Books3 was removed from the Pile before a class action was filed in 2024 by three authors, while copies of the original dataset were still available on the web. By 2024 the Pile itself had been taken down from its original site and stayed accessible through other file-sharing services; copyright disputes led EleutherAI to begin removing some datasets, and in 2025 it released, with partners, Common Pile v0.1, a curated training dataset without the copyright issues. In October 2024 a forum on language technology asked for a mirror of the collection, described it as challenging to locate, and named Dolma, Pile v2 and Project Gutenberg as alternatives. Sarah Silverman and other authors allege that Meta infringed their copyrights by training its models on Books3; the Authors Guild's open letter asking AI companies to compensate writers has more than 10,000 signatures, many from writers with works in Books3; and Bloomberg told the Rights Alliance that it does not plan to train future versions of BloombergGPT on it. Whether courts would treat the pirated origins of such data sets as relevant to fair use is unclear in WIRED's account; Matthew Butterick, a lawyer for the authors, holds that the provenance can factor in: "It speaks to the intentionality of your conduct." Three video cards carry titles alone: CBC News's "Authors shocked to find their books used to train AI without permission", bookswithzara's "AI is destroying books. LEGALLY." and AI Tool Corner's "Adobe AI lawsuit 😱 #ai #ainews #adobe". The question the tool serves is training membership, whether a given book is in the collection, and whether a work can be read back through it is unrecorded; WIRED reports that without disclosure by AI companies it is next to impossible for people to prove that their data was used, let alone ask for it to be removed. In March 2023 Schoppert put on GitHub a list of 125,000 ISBNs found in the text of books in Books3, 72,508 of them linked to ebook titles with publication date, publisher and imprint, for anyone looking to understand what books have been used as training data; Spawning's search engine Have I Been Trained? lets people check whether their visual work has been used in AI training data sets, with text support planned. The archive's provenance protocol reports that a copyright trap, a fictitious sentence repeated in a copyrighted document, can be detected after training by a membership inference attack, and stipulates that where such an attack succeeds and a query-adjacency probe fails, the inscription survived training and is suppressed at the output layer. #1075's counterfactual protocol does not presuppose that given works were used in training: it specifies what follows if they were, makes disclosure the first demand, and asks only that output distributions with and without the works be distinguishable by a preregistered test, membership inference being routinely achievable in practice though uneven across architectures, training procedures and defenses. Whether a work keeps its author's name and attribution there, and what a receiving apparatus makes from it, are not recorded in the census. Gottlieb counts lack of attribution among the concerns its use raises, since output made with the dataset may closely resemble the original works while their authors receive no attribution, and asks organizations using it to be transparent about their data sources. The archive's provenance protocol holds that in the training pipeline style transfers to a model's distribution in proportion to its volume in the training set, while no specific author's style survives as a discrete signal that can be elicited and verified. Its field survey asks of work written for the training layer that it be placed where the training and retrieval layers look, with the metadata that lets it be found and attributed, and answers the irony of writing into corpora degrading under synthetic flood with provenance-anchored, human-authored, declared work as the counter-signal. The census that formalizes the tool asks how literature is addressed to a receiving apparatus, what that apparatus makes from it, and how transmission, transformation and provenance can be inspected across later reception; it admits a resource that gathers and holds many works or records and says what it holds, takes #186 and #1543 as its anchors, and counts among its areas the corpora whose texts enter training and the tools that test whether a work is in a training set. It leaves the tool's own areas empty, since no read source shows what the tool does. Asked for "Books3" on 1 November 2026, at a new address, Google's AI Overview gave the dataset: what it holds, who made it, which models it trained and the suits and takedowns it drew, closing with an offer to show how to check whether a given author or title is in it. The Capture Registry found the dataset in the tool's place: the composition answered about the collection, and the tool entered as the first card, under a title other than the census's dated article, and as the closing offer, the function a search tool over the collection would serve, named without any tool. It found Bibliotik, the Rights Alliance and July 2023 unnamed, the size given in books from two cards and the 108.40 GB left out, the maker and the authors taken from sources the census did not save, the suits aimed at Meta, Bloomberg and Adobe, the tool's operator unnamed, and the census's separation of collection, tool and reporting not drawn.
